recaps.subject: physiology
recaps.title: Cell transport: follow the energy
slides: A gradient needs a pathway.
The sodium–potassium pump spends ATP.
Cotransport uses the stored sodium gradient.
Tonicity depends on effective, non-penetrating solutes.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: Explain how ATP can support glucose uptake without binding to its cotransporter.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: ATP powers the sodium–potassium pump, which maintains a low intracellular sodium concentration. Sodium then enters through a cotransporter down its electrochemical gradient, providing energy for coupled glucose uptake.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: The sodium–potassium pump is inhibited in a teaching model. Why might sodium–glucose uptake weaken later?

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: The sodium gradient gradually becomes less able to power cotransport. The pump maintains the gradient; its loss eventually reduces the energy available to secondary transport.

recaps.subject: physiology
recaps.title: Three muscle types, three calcium stories
slides: Calcium links excitation to force.
Skeletal muscle releases stored calcium through voltage coupling.
Cardiac trigger calcium recruits more calcium release.
Smooth muscle uses calmodulin and myosin light-chain kinase.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: Compare the role of calcium in skeletal, cardiac and smooth muscle.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Skeletal and cardiac muscle use troponin C to regulate actin access. Skeletal coupling primarily releases stored calcium through voltage-sensor coupling; cardiac muscle needs trigger calcium entry. Smooth muscle uses calcium–calmodulin and myosin light-chain kinase to regulate myosin.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: Why can normal skeletal muscle produce tetanic force while normal cardiac working muscle cannot?

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: The cardiac refractory period overlaps much of its contraction. The long refractory period limits repeated excitation and summation into tetanus, preserving filling between beats.

recaps.subject: physiology
recaps.title: Autonomic signals: receptor before response
slides: Begin with the receptor and its location.
Autonomic ganglia use acetylcholine and nicotinic receptors.
M2 signalling helps slow the heart.
The tissue determines what a second messenger does.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: Give a receptor-to-response explanation of slowing at the sinoatrial node.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Acetylcholine activates cardiac M2 receptors. Gi/o signalling reduces cyclic AMP, while beta–gamma subunits can activate GIRK potassium channels. These changes reduce pacemaker activity and slow the heart.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: A learner says every sympathetic postganglionic neuron releases noradrenaline. Which example corrects the claim?

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Sympathetic fibres to eccrine sweat glands release acetylcholine. Eccrine sweat-gland innervation is the important sympathetic cholinergic exception.

recaps.subject: physiology
recaps.title: The cardiac cycle: pressure opens the valves
slides: Valves respond to pressure differences.
Both valves are closed during isovolumetric phases.
Loop width represents stroke volume.
Compare one isolated loading change at a time.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: Predict the immediate effect of an isolated afterload increase on a pressure–volume loop.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: At unchanged preload and contractility, the ventricle must develop more pressure before ejection. It generally ejects less on that beat, leaving a larger end-systolic volume and a narrower loop. Later reflex and filling responses may modify this.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: In a simplified ventricle, end-diastolic volume is 120 mL and end-systolic volume is 50 mL. What is stroke volume?

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: 70 mL. Subtract end-systolic from end-diastolic volume: 120 minus 50 equals 70 mL.

recaps.subject: physiology
recaps.title: Ventilation: make each breath count
slides: Air flows down a pressure difference.
Minute ventilation includes dead space.
Subtract dead space before multiplying by rate.
Equal minute ventilation need not mean equal alveolar ventilation.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: Explain why rapid shallow breaths can be less efficient than slower deeper breaths at the same minute ventilation.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: A fixed conducting-airway volume takes up more of each small breath. After subtracting dead space, less fresh air reaches gas-exchanging alveoli each minute, even when total minute ventilation is unchanged.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: At the same 6 L/min minute ventilation and a fixed 150 mL dead space, which pattern gives greater alveolar ventilation?

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: 500 mL at 12 breaths/min. This gives (500−150)×12 = 4.2 L/min, because less of total ventilation is wasted in dead space.

recaps.subject: physiology
recaps.title: Water balance: distinguish ADH from aldosterone
slides: Ask whether the disturbance concerns volume or osmolality.
ADH inserts aquaporin-2 water channels.
The medullary gradient supplies the driving force.
Aldosterone mainly adjusts sodium and potassium transport.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: Distinguish what ADH changes from what aldosterone changes.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: ADH increases collecting-duct water permeability through aquaporin-2 trafficking. Aldosterone enhances distal sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion. Their effects interact with medullary gradients, intake and circulating-volume signals.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: ADH rises, but the medullary osmotic gradient is greatly reduced. What limits water recovery?

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Increased permeability still needs an osmotic driving force. ADH makes a pathway available; the medullary gradient supplies the driving force.

recaps.subject: physiology
recaps.title: Haemostasis: build and stabilise the plug
slides: Adhesion anchors the first platelets.
Aggregation links activated platelets together.
IXa and VIIIa form intrinsic tenase.
Thrombin generates fibrin; XIIIa crosslinks it.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: Explain the difference between adhesion, aggregation and fibrin stabilisation.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Adhesion anchors platelets to an injured surface. Aggregation joins activated platelets through fibrinogen bridges between alpha-IIb-beta-3 receptors. Coagulation generates thrombin and fibrin, and factor XIIIa crosslinks fibrin to stabilise the plug.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: A student confuses prothrombinase with intrinsic tenase. Which reaction belongs to prothrombinase?

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Prothrombin to thrombin. Xa with Va forms prothrombinase and supports thrombin generation.

recaps.subject: physiology
recaps.title: Digestion: coordinate movement and secretion
slides: Enteric circuits coordinate local responses.
Secretin helps match bicarbonate secretion to acid.
CCK supports enzyme secretion and gallbladder contraction.
Mixing, propulsion and absorption are distinct tasks.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: Explain how a meal containing fat and acid can recruit different pancreatic responses.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Duodenal acid stimulates secretin and bicarbonate-rich ductal secretion. Fat and protein products stimulate cholecystokinin and enzyme-rich secretion, with neural signals coordinating the response. The pathways interact rather than operating as isolated switches.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: Fat enters the duodenum. Which coordinated response fits its digestion?

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: CCK supporting enzyme secretion and gallbladder contraction. CCK helps match enzyme and bile delivery to the incoming nutrient load.

recaps.subject: physiology
recaps.title: Energy balance: connect intake, storage and use
slides: Choose the time interval before discussing energy balance.
Intake and expenditure change stored energy.
The fed state favours nutrient use and storage.
Fasting mobilises stored fuels; water also changes body mass.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: Compare nutrient handling after a meal and during fasting.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: The fed state favours use and storage of absorbed nutrients under a higher insulin signal. Fasting promotes mobilisation of stored fuels and hepatic glucose production under a lower insulin-to-glucagon signal. Energy is transferred and transformed, not created.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: Which statement best connects fasting to ongoing cellular work?

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Stored substrates are mobilised to support continued metabolism. Fasting changes fuel sources while tissues continue to use energy.

recaps.subject: physiology
recaps.title: Endocrine axes: read the feedback loop
slides: Separate hypothalamus, pituitary and target gland.
TRH supports TSH; TSH stimulates the thyroid.
Thyroid hormones reduce upstream stimulation.
Opposite hormone changes can reveal feedback logic.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: Explain why a target-gland hormone and its pituitary signal can move in opposite directions.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: A target-gland hormone can inhibit its upstream control signals. When target-gland secretion falls, reduced negative feedback permits the pituitary signal to rise, provided the central components of the axis remain functional.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: Low thyroid hormone is accompanied by a TSH that is not appropriately elevated. What does this challenge in a simple model?

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: The assumption that the central feedback response is intact. An intact pituitary response to primary thyroid failure would usually raise TSH; central influences merit consideration.

recaps.subject: physiology
recaps.title: Reproductive physiology: connect the two cycles
slides: Gonadotrophins coordinate gonadal function.
Follicular estradiol supports endometrial growth.
Sustained high estradiol can trigger the LH surge.
Luteal progesterone supports the secretory endometrium.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: Relate the ovarian and endometrial phases without assuming a fixed calendar.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Follicular estradiol supports endometrial proliferation. A sustained estradiol rise can trigger an LH surge and ovulation. Luteal progesterone supports secretory endometrium; falling luteal hormones contribute to menstruation when pregnancy does not maintain the corpus luteum.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: After ovulation, which hormone most directly supports secretory differentiation of the endometrium?

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Progesterone from the corpus luteum. Luteal progesterone supports secretory changes following estradiol-driven proliferation.

recaps.subject: physiology
recaps.title: Neural integration: from release to a response
slides: An arriving action potential opens presynaptic calcium channels.
Calcium triggers vesicle fusion.
Receptors change postsynaptic signalling or conductance.
Inputs combine across both time and space.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: Distinguish chemical transmission from temporal and spatial summation.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Chemical transmission releases a transmitter that changes postsynaptic signalling or conductance. Temporal summation combines closely timed inputs; spatial summation combines inputs at different sites. Their combined effect helps determine whether the receiving neuron fires.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: Repeated small inputs at the same synapse arrive close together and have a larger combined effect. What is this?

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Temporal summation. Temporal summation combines effects of closely timed inputs.

recaps.subject: physiology
recaps.title: Special senses: convert a stimulus into a signal
slides: Sensory receptors transform physical stimuli.
Light hyperpolarises rods and cones.
Excitatory hair-bundle movement depolarises hair cells.
A graded receptor response can control transmitter release.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: Compare the direction of the initial receptor response to light and to excitatory hair-bundle deflection.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Light closes cyclic-GMP-gated channels and hyperpolarises a photoreceptor. Excitatory hair-bundle deflection opens mechanically gated channels and depolarises a hair cell. Both graded responses regulate transmitter release.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: A hair bundle is deflected in its excitatory direction. Which initial response is expected?

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Opening of mechanotransduction channels and depolarisation. Mechanical channel opening permits a depolarising current under the inner-ear ionic conditions.

recaps.subject: physiology
recaps.title: Microcirculation: return the filtered fluid
slides: Filtration depends on forces and the endothelial barrier.
Lymphatics return filtered fluid and proteins.
Venous-end reabsorption is not universal.
Name the changed mechanism before explaining oedema.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: Explain how venous pressure and lymphatic obstruction can both produce fluid accumulation.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Higher venous pressure can increase capillary hydrostatic pressure and filtration. Lymphatic obstruction reduces the route that returns filtered fluid and proteins. Both can increase interstitial fluid, but through different parts of the balance.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: Two examples cause oedema: increased venous pressure and lymphatic obstruction. What differs?

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: One can increase filtration; the other reduces return. They change different sides of the filtration–return balance.

recaps.subject: anatomy
recaps.title: Volume I: orient the thorax around the lung root
slides: Use the sternal angle to establish orientation.
The phrenic nerve passes anterior to the lung root.
The vagus passes posterior to the root.
Phrenic motor fibres chiefly come from C3 to C5.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: Orient the two nerves at the lung root and connect one to its main motor target.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: The phrenic nerve runs anterior to the lung root and supplies the diaphragm through fibres principally from C3–C5. The vagus runs posterior to the root and contributes to thoracic autonomic networks.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: A diagram places the diaphragm low in the thorax. Why does this not imply thoracic motor roots?

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Its phrenic motor supply principally comes from C3–C5. Adult position and developmental history must be distinguished from segmental motor supply.

recaps.subject: anatomy
recaps.title: Volume II: connect peritoneum and the portal triad
slides: Peritoneal covering and attachment are distinct relationships.
The portal triad lies in the hepatoduodenal ligament.
The portal vein is posterior to the duct–artery pair.
Gut development helps explain adult attachments and territories.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: Describe the portal triad while distinguishing the figure's main relationship from its simplification.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: The portal vein is posterior; the bile duct and proper hepatic artery are anterior. Conventionally the duct is right and artery left from the patient's perspective. The figure is a front–back relationship schematic rather than a complete operative view.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: In a conventional anterior view of the portal triad, where is the bile duct relative to the proper hepatic artery?

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: On the patient's right. The duct conventionally lies to the patient's right of the proper hepatic artery; variants exist.

recaps.subject: anatomy
recaps.title: Volume III: follow urine through the pelvis
slides: Keep the blood and urinary routes separate.
Calyces lead to the renal pelvis and ureter.
The ureter reaches the bladder; the urethra leaves it.
Nephrons and the collecting system develop from interacting tissues.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: Connect the urinary route to its two renal developmental components.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Nephrons derived from metanephric mesenchyme connect to the collecting system derived from the ureteric bud. Urine passes through collecting ducts to calyces, renal pelvis, ureter and bladder, then exits through the urethra.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: Which developmental pairing is correct?

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Ureteric bud forms the collecting system; metanephric mesenchyme forms nephrons. Reciprocal interaction between these tissues connects nephrons to the collecting system.

recaps.subject: anatomy
recaps.title: Volume IV: separate taste, sensation and movement
slides: First name the territory and sensory modality.
Anterior general sensation mainly uses V3.
Most anterior taste uses VII; posterior taste uses IX.
Most tongue movement uses XII, with palatoglossus as an exception.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: Explain why a single tongue map cannot replace a modality-specific answer.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: General sensation, taste and movement use different pathways. Most anterior general sensation uses V3, anterior taste uses VII, posterior sensation and taste use IX, and most motor supply uses XII. Circumvallate papillae and palatoglossus are important exceptions.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: Which exception should accompany an anterior-versus-posterior tongue taste map?

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Circumvallate papillae receive taste fibres from IX. Circumvallate papillae lie just anterior to the terminal sulcus but have IX taste innervation.

recaps.subject: anatomy
recaps.title: Volume V: trace a limb nerve through the plexus
slides: Follow roots, trunks, divisions, cords and branches.
The usual roots are ventral rami C5 to T1.
Cord names refer to the axillary artery.
Explain movement with the muscle, joint and nerve together.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: Trace C5–T1 through the plexus and explain how the cords are named.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Ventral rami C5–T1 form upper, middle and lower trunks, each dividing into anterior and posterior divisions. These combine into lateral, medial and posterior cords, named relative to the second part of the axillary artery, and then give terminal branches.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: A diagram labels the posterior cord. Posterior relative to what?

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: The second part of the axillary artery. The artery provides the conventional landmark for brachial-plexus cord names.

recaps.subject: histology
recaps.title: Epithelia: layers, shape and function
slides: Distinguish simple, stratified and pseudostratified epithelia and connect their structure to their job.
Find the two surfaces
Count layers, then name the surface cells
Connect architecture to function

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: Why does alveolar epithelium differ from esophageal epithelium?

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Alveoli need a short diffusion distance and use thin squamous cells. The esophagus resists abrasion with a nonkeratinized stratified squamous lining.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: A section has nuclei at different heights, but every cell contacts the basal lamina. Which interpretation fits?

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Pseudostratified epithelium is possible. In pseudostratified epithelium all cells contact the basal lamina, although not all reach the surface.

recaps.subject: cell-biology
recaps.title: PCR, qPCR and reverse transcription
slides: Distinguish amplification, real-time measurement and the conversion of RNA to DNA.
Define the target
Distinguish the abbreviations
Interpret with controls

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: What does a positive no-template control suggest?

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: It suggests contamination or nonspecific signal and requires investigation before interpreting the samples. It is not evidence of a true target in every specimen.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: A PCR tube lacks one of the two primers. What is the main consequence for the intended target?

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Efficient exponential amplification of the bounded target is lost. The two primers define opposite ends and support amplification of both strands.

recaps.subject: biochemistry
recaps.title: Enzyme catalysis and inhibition
slides: Separate reaction rate from equilibrium and compare substrate competition with loss of catalytic capacity.
Change the route, not the equilibrium
Read a saturation curve
State the inhibition model

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: Why can adding enzyme accelerate a reaction without changing its final equilibrium?

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Catalysis lowers the kinetic barrier for forward and reverse reaction paths. It changes how quickly equilibrium is reached, not the relative free energies of reactants and products.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: In a simple reversible competitive-inhibition model, what can increasing substrate concentration do?

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Reduce the inhibitor's effect on the observed rate. Substrate competes for binding; sufficiently high substrate can approach the same Vmax in the ideal model.

recaps.subject: genetics
recaps.title: Complement pathways and their shared effectors
slides: Follow three initiation routes toward opsonization, inflammation and terminal complex formation.
Converge on C3
Separate the outputs
Protect host tissue

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: Explain why activating complement and limiting complement are both necessary.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Activation labels and attacks targets and recruits responses. Regulation limits amplification and terminal injury on host surfaces, preserving useful defense without uncontrolled tissue damage.

dialogue.speaker: Host
dialogue.text: Why can different complement activation pathways have common downstream effects?

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: They converge on C3 activation and shared downstream components. Convergence explains shared effects such as C3b-mediated opsonisation despite different triggers.
